lessonTitle: DNA Methylation, Histone Modification and Imprinting

blocks.text: Two children each carry a missing piece of the same stretch of chromosome 15. One was floppy and fed poorly as a baby, then became relentlessly hungry and obese. The other has severe developmental delay, no speech, an unsteady gait and frequent smiling and laughter. The difference lies not in the size of the deletion but in which parent it came from.

blocks.markdown: **Epigenetics** is the study of heritable changes in gene expression that occur *without* a change in the DNA base sequence. The DNA sequence is the same in every cell of the body, yet a neuron and a hepatocyte express different genes. Epigenetic marks, which are chemical modifications on DNA and on the histone proteins around which it is wrapped, determine which genes are accessible. These marks can be copied when cells divide, so they allow cell identity to be remembered, and they can be altered by development and environment.

blocks.title: DNA methylation
blocks.text: DNA methylation is the addition of a methyl group to carbon 5 of cytosine (forming 5-methylcytosine) by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), mostly where a cytosine is followed by a guanine (a CpG dinucleotide). Dense methylation of CpG islands in a gene's promoter typically silences the gene.

blocks.markdown: **How methylation silences genes.** CpG islands are CG-rich regions, found at the promoters of many genes. In an active gene the promoter CpG island is unmethylated. When it is methylated, methyl-CpG-binding proteins (for example MeCP2) bind and recruit histone deacetylases and other repressors, and transcription factors can no longer bind, so the gene is switched off. Maintenance methyltransferase (DNMT1) copies the pattern onto the new strand after replication, because newly replicated DNA is hemimethylated; this is why the mark is heritable through cell division. Methylation is abnormal in many cancers: for instance, aberrant promoter methylation can silence tumour-suppressor genes.

**Histone modification.** DNA is wound around octamers of histones to form nucleosomes. The positively charged tails of histones, particularly lysine residues, can be chemically modified. **Histone acetylation** by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) neutralises the positive charge of lysine, loosening the contact with the negatively charged DNA; chromatin becomes open (euchromatin) and genes are more accessible and expressed. **Histone deacetylases (HDACs)** remove the acetyl groups, restoring the positive charge, so chromatin compacts (heterochromatin) and transcription falls. Histone **methylation** can either activate or repress depending on the residue (for example, trimethylation of lysine 4 on histone H3 is a mark of active promoters, whereas trimethylation of lysine 9 or 27 marks repressed chromatin). Methylated DNA and deacetylated histones act together to maintain a silent state.

blocks.title: Genomic imprinting
blocks.text: Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic process in which a small number of genes are expressed from only one allele, determined by the parent of origin. In an imprinted gene the allele from one parent is silenced by methylation, so the individual is functionally hemizygous. Imprints are erased in the germline and re-established according to the sex of the person in whom the germ cells develop.

blocks.markdown: **Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes.** These two distinct disorders map to the same region on the long arm of chromosome 15 (15q11-q13), which contains imprinted genes. In this region some genes are expressed only from the paternal chromosome, and the **UBE3A** gene is expressed in neurons only from the *maternal* chromosome. **Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS)** results from loss of the *paternal* contribution of the region: about 70% have a paternal deletion, about 25% have maternal uniparental disomy (both copies of chromosome 15 from the mother), and a small number have an imprinting defect. Features are neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding, then hyperphagia with obesity from early childhood, hypogonadism, short stature and mild learning disability. **Angelman syndrome (AS)** results from loss of the *maternal* UBE3A function: a maternal deletion of 15q11-q13 in roughly 70%, paternal uniparental disomy, an imprinting defect, or a mutation in maternal UBE3A. Features are severe developmental delay, absent or minimal speech, ataxia, seizures, microcephaly and a happy demeanour with frequent laughter. Diagnosis begins with DNA methylation testing at the region, which detects deletions, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects.

blocks.title: Deducing the syndrome from the mechanism
blocks.prompt: Three infants with 15q11-q13 abnormalities: (A) a deletion on the paternal chromosome 15; (B) two maternal chromosome 15 copies and no paternal copy (maternal uniparental disomy); (C) a deletion on the maternal chromosome 15. Which syndrome does each have?

steps.text: Prader-Willi syndrome results from absence of the paternally expressed genes in 15q11-q13. The key question is whether a functional paternal copy is present.
Infant A has lost the paternal region, and the maternal copy is silenced by imprinting, so no paternally derived gene product is made: Prader-Willi syndrome.

Infant B has no paternal chromosome 15 at all, and both maternal copies are imprinted in the same way, so no paternally expressed genes are available: Prader-Willi syndrome, even though the amount of DNA is normal.
Infant C has lost the maternal chromosome. The paternal UBE3A allele is silenced in neurons, so no UBE3A is made: Angelman syndrome.

blocks.answer: A and B have Prader-Willi syndrome; C has Angelman syndrome.

rows: Maternal deletion (about 70%), paternal UPD, imprinting defect, UBE3A mutation
Delayed milestones, feeding generally less affected
Hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism, mild learning disability
Severe developmental delay, absent speech, ataxia, seizures, happy demeanour

blocks.markdown: **X-chromosome inactivation (Lyon hypothesis).** Females have two X chromosomes and males have one, which would give females twice the dose of X-linked gene products. Dosage is equalised because, in each cell of a female embryo, one X is almost completely silenced (**dosage compensation**). Inactivation begins in the early embryo (about the blastocyst stage), when each cell *randomly* chooses one X (maternal or paternal) to inactivate. A non-coding RNA called **XIST**, transcribed from the future inactive X, coats that chromosome and recruits repressive complexes, including DNA methylation and histone modification; the X condenses into a **Barr body** visible at the nuclear periphery. The choice is then stably inherited by all descendants of the cell, so adult females are **mosaics** of two cell populations, one expressing maternal X genes and one paternal. A few genes on the inactive X escape silencing. The mosaicism explains why heterozygous female carriers of X-linked recessive disease may show mild or variable features, especially if inactivation is *skewed* toward the normal X.

blocks.title: Skewed X-inactivation in a carrier
blocks.prompt: A female carries a loss-of-function mutation on her maternal X. In a skin sample, 30% of cells express the maternal X and 70% express the paternal X. What fraction of her cells express the mutant allele, and what would you predict about disease expression compared with a carrier whose inactivation is 50:50?

steps.text: Cells with the maternal X active express the mutant allele: 30%.
At 50:50, half the cells would express the mutant allele, so this carrier has fewer mutant-expressing cells and would be expected to be less affected than the 50:50 carrier.

blocks.answer: 30% of cells express the mutant allele; she is expected to have milder or no disease compared with a 50:50 carrier.

blocks.title: Epigenetic marks are reversible and heritable through cell division
blocks.text: Unlike mutations, epigenetic changes do not alter the DNA sequence and can in principle be reversed (for example, HDAC inhibitors are used as cancer drugs, which is a pharmacology teaching example). Imprinting and X-inactivation show that silencing can be maintained for the lifetime of the individual.

points: Promoter CpG methylation and histone deacetylation silence genes; histone acetylation opens chromatin and promotes transcription.
Imprinting silences one parental allele; Prader-Willi syndrome is loss of paternal 15q11-q13 function and Angelman syndrome is loss of maternal UBE3A function.
X-inactivation randomly silences one X in each female cell early in development via XIST RNA, equalising X-gene dosage between the sexes and making females mosaics.

questions.stem: Which change to chromatin is most likely to increase transcription of a gene?

options.text: Acetylation of histone tails by histone acetyltransferases
Methylation of CpG islands in the promoter
Removal of acetyl groups by histone deacetylases
Binding of MeCP2 to the promoter

questions.correctOptionText: Acetylation of histone tails by histone acetyltransferases

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acetylation reduces histone-DNA affinity, opening chromatin.
distractorRationale.c: HDACs compact chromatin and reduce transcription.
distractorRationale.d: MeCP2 binds methylated DNA and recruits repressors.

questions.explanation: Acetylation neutralises the positive charge of lysines on the histone tails, weakening their binding to DNA and opening chromatin for transcription. Methylation of promoter CpG islands and histone deacetylation have the opposite effect.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with global developmental delay, ataxia, seizures and frequent laughter has a methylation study that shows loss of the maternal pattern at 15q11-q13 with two paternal copies of chromosome 15 and no maternal copy. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Paternal uniparental disomy causing Angelman syndrome
Paternal uniparental disomy causing Prader-Willi syndrome
Maternal uniparental disomy causing Angelman syndrome
Trisomy 15 with mosaicism

questions.correctOptionText: Paternal uniparental disomy causing Angelman syndrome

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with no maternal copy there is no maternal UBE3A expression, so Angelman syndrome results.
distractorRationale.b: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternal genes, i.e. maternal UPD or paternal deletion.
distractorRationale.c: Maternal UPD causes Prader-Willi, not Angelman.
distractorRationale.d: Two copies of chromosome 15 are present, so this is uniparental disomy, not trisomy.

questions.explanation: UBE3A is expressed in neurons only from the maternal chromosome. A child with two paternal chromosome 15s has no maternally derived UBE3A expression, so Angelman syndrome results.

questions.stem: A male infant is markedly hypotonic and feeds poorly. At 3 years he is constantly seeking food and is obese. Which genetic finding is most likely?

options.text: Deletion of paternal 15q11-q13
Deletion of maternal 15q11-q13
A trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1
Trisomy 21

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Prader-Willi syndrome most commonly results from a paternal deletion.
distractorRationale.b: A maternal deletion causes Angelman syndrome.
distractorRationale.c: FMR1 expansions cause fragile X syndrome, which has a different phenotype.
distractorRationale.d: Trisomy 21 does not produce hyperphagia and obesity as a main feature.

questions.explanation: Neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding followed by hyperphagia and obesity describe Prader-Willi syndrome. It arises from absence of paternally expressed 15q11-q13 genes, most often through a paternal deletion.

questions.stem: Which statement about X-chromosome inactivation in a normal 46,XX female is correct?

options.text: In early embryonic cells one X is randomly inactivated and the choice is passed to all daughter cells
The paternal X is always inactivated in all somatic cells
Both X chromosomes are inactive in every cell
The inactive X is re-activated in every cell division

questions.correctOptionText: In early embryonic cells one X is randomly inactivated and the choice is passed to all daughter cells

distractorRationale.a: Correct: random inactivation followed by clonal maintenance makes females mosaic.
distractorRationale.b: In the human embryo proper inactivation is random, not always paternal.
distractorRationale.c: One X remains active in each cell.
distractorRationale.d: Inactivation is stably maintained through cell division.

questions.explanation: Each cell randomly chooses one X to inactivate early in embryogenesis, mediated by XIST RNA and repressive chromatin changes. The inactive X is stably inherited by daughter cells, so females are mosaics for their two X chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which statement about genomic imprinting is correct?

options.text: An imprinted gene is expressed from only one parental allele, so a single mutation or deletion of the active allele can cause disease
Imprints are permanent and never erased in the germline
Imprinting changes the DNA base sequence of the silenced allele
Imprinted genes are expressed from both alleles equally

questions.correctOptionText: An imprinted gene is expressed from only one parental allele, so a single mutation or deletion of the active allele can cause disease

distractorRationale.a: Correct: functional hemizygosity makes the single active allele critical.
distractorRationale.b: Imprints are erased in germ cells and re-set according to the sex of the individual.
distractorRationale.c: Imprinting is epigenetic and does not change the sequence.
distractorRationale.d: By definition imprinted genes show monoallelic, parent-of-origin-specific expression.

questions.explanation: Because the allele from one parent is silenced, only one allele is active, so loss of that allele cannot be compensated. The imprint is an epigenetic mark (methylation), erased and re-set in the germline.

questions.stem: A woman is heterozygous for a mutation causing X-linked deficiency of an enzyme, with the mutation on her paternal X. A tissue biopsy shows that the paternal X is the active X in 85% of the cells. Assuming enzyme activity is proportional to the fraction of cells in which the normal allele is active, what percentage of normal enzyme activity would you expect? Give your answer in percent (%).
questions.explanation: Cells with the paternal (mutant) X active make no functional enzyme. Only cells in which the maternal X is active express the normal allele: 100% - 85% = 15%. This is skewed X-inactivation, which can make a female carrier symptomatic.

questions.stem: True or false: Hypermethylation of a gene's promoter CpG island usually increases its expression.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Hypermethylation of promoter CpG islands recruits methyl-CpG-binding proteins and histone deacetylases and blocks transcription factor binding, so it usually silences the gene.

questions.stem: Describe how DNA methylation and histone acetylation each alter gene expression, and explain how these marks can be maintained through cell division.
markingGuide: DNA methylation: methyl group added to cytosine at CpG by DNMTs; methylated promoter CpG islands silence genes by recruiting methyl-CpG-binding proteins (e.g. MeCP2) and HDACs and blocking transcription factor binding.
Histone acetylation by HATs neutralises lysine's positive charge, loosening DNA-histone contact, giving open chromatin and increased transcription.
Histone deacetylation by HDACs compacts chromatin and reduces transcription.
Maintenance: DNMT1 copies methylation onto the new strand of hemimethylated DNA after replication.
Marks do not change DNA sequence and can be reversed.
questions.explanation: Methylation and deacetylation together form a silent chromatin state, while acetylation promotes an open active state. DNMT1 faithfully copies methylation after replication.

questions.stem: Explain what genomic imprinting is, and use it to explain why a deletion of 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome when paternally inherited but Angelman syndrome when maternally inherited.
markingGuide: Imprinting is parent-of-origin-specific silencing (by methylation) of one allele so that only one allele is expressed.
Imprints are erased in the germline and re-established according to the sex of the parent.
Prader-Willi: genes in 15q11-q13 are normally expressed only from the paternal chromosome; paternal deletion (or maternal UPD) removes all paternal expression.
Angelman: UBE3A is expressed in neurons only from the maternal chromosome; maternal deletion, paternal UPD, UBE3A mutation or imprinting defect removes it.
Same region, different parental origin of the missing copy, so different phenotypes.
questions.explanation: The same chromosomal deletion has different effects depending on which parent's copy is lost, because the remaining copy is silenced by imprinting. This is the hallmark of imprinted disorders.

questions.stem: State how X-chromosome inactivation equalises gene dosage between males and females, describing the role of XIST and the consequences for a heterozygous female carrier of an X-linked recessive condition.
markingGuide: One X in each female somatic cell is silenced early in development so that females, like males, have effectively one active X.
Inactivation is random between maternal and paternal X in each early cell, then clonally inherited.
XIST non-coding RNA is transcribed from the inactive X and coats it, recruiting repressive complexes including DNA methylation and histone modification; the X becomes a Barr body.
Females are mosaics of two cell populations.
A carrier may be unaffected or mildly affected because of the normal X active in many cells; skewed inactivation toward the normal X reduces, and toward the mutant X increases, expression of disease.
questions.explanation: Dosage compensation silences one X per cell, so both sexes have a single active X. Random inactivation makes carriers mosaic and explains variable manifestation.
